title: The Alien Gambit: the idea and the first six moves
outcomes: Says why White plays Ng5 on move five and why f7 is the target: it is defended once, by the king, while h7 is defended twice
Names the six squares a knight on f7 attacks, sees that it forks the queen and a rook, and explains why Black must capture it with the king
States honestly that the sacrifice is objectively unsound (engine, depth 20: Black about two pawns ahead) yet practically testing, with our own sample sizes
Steps through the first moves and a typical continuation, with the purpose of each move, and reads two real games
Names the typical mistakes for each side (...Bg4 or ...Ke7 for Black, Qh5+ for White) and the reason each fails

steps.caption: White to move. Black's pawn on h6 attacks the knight on g5, and only the bishop on c1 defends it. White can retreat the knight, or look at f7. Which black pieces would a knight on f7 attack?

claims.statement: One black piece (the h6 pawn) attacks g5.
One white piece (the bishop on c1) defends g5.
Taking on f7 is legal.

steps.prompt: Before reading on: would you retreat the knight, or take on f7? Write one reason.

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The Alien Gambit gives a knight for a pawn on move six. Why would anyone do that, what does the knight attack on f7, and what does each side get? By the end you can answer in your own words, say honestly whether it is sound, and set up the first moves on a board. Marks: [V] checked, [S] source, [R] recalled, [I] inference, [H] guess.

steps.caption: The setting, step by step. White opens with the e-pawn, Black prepares ...d5 with the c-pawn, and White adds a second central pawn. Step through and say each purpose aloud. [I] The purposes are my reading.

line.say: White takes space and opens lines for the queen and the bishop.
Black prepares ...d5, supported by the c-pawn.
White adds a second central pawn.

steps.chapter: Move five: why the knight goes to g5

steps.prompt: Black's d-pawn will strike at the pawn on e4. Predict how White meets that, and who ends up with the extra pawn for a moment.

steps.caption: Black strikes at the e4 pawn at once. White defends it with a knight, and Black takes the pawn. Before you step: how would White win the pawn back?

line.say: Black strikes at the e4 pawn at once.
The knight defends e4 and develops.
Black wins the pawn and opens the d-file.

steps.caption: White takes back with a piece, and Black's knight attacks it. After the last move, which white piece is loose, and who attacks it? [I] The purposes are my reading.

line.say: White takes back with a piece and keeps the centre.
Black attacks the knight on e4 and develops with it.

claims.statement: After the two moves, the knight on e4 is White's only loose piece.
After the two moves, one black piece attacks e4.

steps.caption: White's usual answer is to trade on f6. [V] At depth 20 the position after the trade is worth about +0.3 pawns for White. Black takes back with the e-pawn and the pawns on f6 and f7 are doubled.

line.say: White trades the attacked knight for Black's developed one, with check.
Black takes back; the f-pawns are doubled.

claims.statement: After 5.Nxf6+ the engine value is between 0 and +0.7 pawns for White (depth 20).
After Nxf6+ exf6, Black's pawns on f6 and f7 are doubled.

steps.caption: The gambit player does something else. 5.Ng5 moves the knight away from the attack and aims it at f7 and h7. [V] At depth 20 the engine rates the position about level, a few tenths of a pawn worse for White than the trade. Engine numbers wobble by about two tenths from run to run. It is playable, not a blunder.

line.say: The knight escapes, keeps both knights on the board and attacks f7 and h7.

claims.statement: After 5.Ng5 the knight attacks exactly these squares.
After 5.Ng5 the engine value is between -0.6 and +0.1 pawns for White (depth 20).

steps.caption: Count the defenders. On f7: one attacker (the knight), one defender (the king). On h7: one attacker, two defenders. A capture on h7 would lose the knight for a pawn, so f7 is the only real target. Taking on f7 loses the knight to the king, unless the knight does enough damage first. Does it?

claims.statement: One white piece attacks f7.
One black piece defends f7.
One white piece attacks h7.
Two black pieces defend h7.

steps.caption: Black's most common reply in our online data is a pawn move that attacks the knight. [V] Online counts (Lichess, Sept 2026, 2,299 games after 5.Ng5): ...h6 was played in 1,041 games, 45%. It takes the square g5 away, so White must decide at once.

line.say: The pawn attacks the knight, which now has to decide.

claims.statement: After ...h6 one black piece attacks g5.
The knight on g5 attacks exactly these squares.

steps.caption: White's quiet answer keeps every piece. [V] At depth 20 the retreat is the engine's first choice and the position is level to slightly better for Black. In our online data only 129 of the 1,041 games went this way.

line.say: The knight retreats to the centre and eyes e5.
Black hits the d4 pawn.
The pawn supports d4 and keeps the centre.

claims.statement: The retreat to f3 is within 40 cp of the engine's top move (depth 16).

steps.caption: The sacrifice: 6.Nxf7. From f7 the knight attacks six squares: d8, h8, d6, h6, e5 and g5. The queen stands on d8, a rook on h8, a pawn on h6. One knight attacks three black units, and Black has one clearly good answer. Look at the arrows.

claims.statement: The knight on f7 attacks exactly these squares.
The knight on f7 is White's only loose piece.
The rook on h8 is Black's only loose piece.

steps.caption: Suppose Black ignores the fork with 6...Bf5?. The knight takes the queen. The king recaptures, but Black has lost a queen for a knight.

line.say: The knight takes the queen.
The king recaptures: Black has lost a queen for a knight.

claims.statement: Nxd8 nets White at least five points of material.

steps.caption: Suppose the queen moves away instead, 6...Qd5. Then the knight takes the rook on h8. [V] The other replies we checked (Qd5, Bg4 and Bf5) each lose at least four pawns more than taking the knight (depth 16).

line.say: The knight takes the rook; White is now ahead in material.

claims.statement: Nxh8 nets White at least one point of material along the engine's line.

steps.caption: So Black takes the knight with the king. White has given a knight (3) for a pawn (1): two pawns. The king stands on f7 and has left e8, so it cannot castle. [V] At depth 20 the engine rates the position at about two pawns for Black.

line.say: The knight takes a pawn and forks the queen and a rook.
The king takes the knight; Black is a piece up for a pawn.

claims.statement: Along the engine's line White nets between -3 and -1 in material.
After 6...Kxf7 the engine value is between -2.6 and -1.5 pawns for White (depth 20).
The black king stands on f7 after the capture.

steps.prompt: A knight for a pawn is a big price. What would White need in return for this to be worth trying? Write two things.

steps.text: **What White hopes to buy.** [I] Time: the king on f7 makes checks gain tempi. Lines: the bishop's diagonal to f7 is open. Squares: a knight on e5 gives check. And surprise: Black must find several accurate moves in a row. None of these is a pawn, so the gambit is a bet on the next few moves, not an investment with a return.

steps.caption: One way White uses the tempi. [I] White develops, Black attacks d4, and White develops again with check. What must Black do about the check?

line.say: Develops and prepares Ne5 with check.
Black attacks the d4 pawn.
Develops with check; the king must react.

claims.statement: Nf3 and Bc4+ are each within 40 cp of the top move (depth 16).

steps.caption: Black blocks with the pawn, and the knight then checks from e5 and the king steps to g8. [I] Each white move develops a piece or gives check, so Black never gets a quiet move to untangle.

line.say: Black blocks the check with a pawn.
The knight gives check from the centre.
The king steps to g8. It has already moved, so it cannot castle.

claims.statement: After this line the engine value is between -2.6 and -1.3 pawns for White (depth 20).

steps.caption: A second route: the bishop check first. After the check the e-pawn blocks, and the queen develops to e2.

line.say: Develops with check at once.
Black blocks the check with the e-pawn.
The queen develops next to the bishop.

claims.statement: Nf3 and Bc4+ are each within 40 cp of the top move (depth 16).
After 7.Bc4+ the engine value is between -2.6 and -1.5 pawns for White (depth 20).

steps.caption: The verdict. [V] After the best moves of both sides the engine, at depth 20, has Black ahead by about two pawns: close to the net material White gave, a knight for a pawn. So the gambit is objectively unsound. [I] But that is a statement about perfect defence. Online, nobody defends perfectly in a few seconds.

claims.statement: The engine value is between -2.6 and -1.5 pawns for White (depth 20).

steps.caption: What people actually do. [V] Online (Lichess, Sept 2026, 4.75 million games): after 5...h6, 901 White players took on f7 and 129 retreated. After the capture White scored 51.6% (wins plus half the draws, over 901 games). Online amateur data is not master theory.

claims.statement: Taking on f7 is legal.
Retreating to f3 is legal.

steps.prompt: White scored 51.6% over 901 online games with the sacrifice. Does that show the sacrifice is sound?

fields.label: My answer:
options: yes, a score over 50% means it works
no, a score mixes strength, speed and surprise

steps.text: **Strength matters more than the opening.** [V] On Lichess, a band is the average rating of both players. White scored about 46% over 308 games where the two averaged 1900 or more, and about 57% over 158 games where they averaged below 1500.

**The rating gap in our archive.** [S] Our archive holds 226 games from titled-player and other events, mostly online blitz. White scored 48% overall: about 65% over 78 games when White was rated 50 or more points higher, about 34% over 106 when Black was. [I] The rating gap swamped the opening.

steps.caption: A real game [S: TWIC issue 1523, event "Titled Tue 9th Jan Early", 2024; the move list is the only source we hold]. White: Volen Dyulgerov (2200). Black: S. Glashausser (1973). Step through and name each purpose before you read it. [I] The purposes are my reading.

line.say: The knight develops and prepares Ne5 with check.
Black opens the bishop's diagonal and covers the d5 square.
The bishop aims at the kingside, where the black king stands.

claims.statement: 7.Nf3 is legal here.

steps.caption: The same game, a few moves later. Black has developed both queenside pieces. Where is White aiming, and what does the bishop on d3 look at?

line.say: Black develops and adds a guard to the knight on f6.
White castles; the rook will come to e1.
Black develops the bishop towards the kingside.

steps.caption: The same game, the next stage. White brings a rook to e1, Black answers, and the knight checks from e5. Say why the knight on e5 is safe.

line.say: The rook supports the knight's jump to e5.
The rook leaves the corner and guards e6.
The knight gives check; it is defended by the d4 pawn and the rook.

claims.statement: 10.Re1 is legal here.

steps.caption: The king goes to g8, the queen swings over and Black covers h7. What might White sacrifice on h6, and why?

line.say: The king goes to g8, still unable to castle.
The queen swings over, preparing a bishop sacrifice on h6.
The knight steps back to cover h7 and g6.

steps.caption: The bishop takes the pawn on h6 to drag the g-pawn away from the king. Black takes the bishop, and the g-file in front of the king is open.

line.say: The bishop takes the pawn on h6 to drag the g-pawn away from the king.
Black takes the bishop; the g-file is now open in front of the king.

steps.caption: The finish [S]. The queen gives check, Black's king runs to the corner, and the knight returns to f7: the square where the sacrifice happened.

line.say: The queen checks along the g-file.
The king goes to the corner (Black could have tried ...Ng6 instead).
The knight gives mate in the corner.

claims.statement: After Qg3+ Kh8, Nf7 is mate.

steps.caption: A second real game, with the other result [S: TWIC issue 1579, 4 Feb 2025; White Kuandykuly (2151), Black Tisaj (2424)]. Black develops, trades White's active pieces and wins the d4 pawn.

line.say: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain.
The knight checks the king.
The king steps aside.

steps.caption: White offers a trade of bishops, Black guards f5 and opens its own bishop, and White takes on f5. What should Black take back with?

line.say: White offers a trade of the bishops.
Black guards f5 and opens the f8 bishop.
White takes the bishop.

steps.caption: Black takes back with the pawn and the e-file opens. The queen then attacks f5 and Black takes the d4 pawn. [I] The gambit gives White play only while Black's pieces are uncoordinated.

line.say: Black takes back; the e-file opens.
The queen attacks f5.
Black takes the d4 pawn, centralising the queen.

claims.statement: After this line the engine value is at most -2.5 pawns for White (depth 16).

steps.text: **Credit.** [S] Volen Dyulgerov is the White player in the first game above; the second game is Kuandykuly-Tisaj. Our archive holds 30 of his games with the line as White (13 wins, 14 losses, 3 draws) [V], not all his games. Who first played it is not settled [I]. This lesson is our own wording, built from move lists, engine checks and our own counts.

steps.caption: The commonest Black error in our data. [V] After 7.Nf3 online (745 games), ...Bg4 was played 129 times and White scored 79.8%, against about 40% after ...c5 or ...e6. The reason is on the board. The bishop on g4 is attacked twice, by the knight on e5 and the queen on d1, and guarded once, by the knight on f6.

line.say: The bishop develops and attacks the knight on f3, which looks natural.
The knight jumps away with check and attacks the bishop on g4.
The king steps away; the bishop is still attacked.
White takes the bishop. If the knight retakes, the queen retakes: two attackers beat one defender.

claims.statement: ...Bg4 is at least 150 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).
After 7...Bg4 8.Ne5+ Ke8, two white pieces attack g4.
After 7...Bg4 8.Ne5+ Ke8, one black piece (the knight on f6) guards g4.

steps.caption: A second trap, this time for the king. After 7...e6 8.Ne5+ the king has three squares. Only one is good. [V] Depth 16: ...Kg8 holds, ...Ke8 is clearly worse, and ...Ke7? allows a fork.

line.say: The king steps to the centre, which looks active.
The knight checks the king and attacks the rook on h8.
The king steps back.
White wins the rook.

claims.statement: ...Ke7 is at least 400 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).

steps.caption: The commonest White error. A queen check looks natural and is not: the knight on f6 guards h5. [I] Checks are only good when you have counted what guards the square.

line.say: The queen gives check from the d1-h5 diagonal.
The knight captures the queen for free.

claims.statement: Qh5+ is at least 500 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).
One black piece (the knight on f6) attacks h5.

steps.title: Does the knight attack the queen?
steps.prompt: Predict for each position, then check. One change matters; one does not.

steps.caption: Why the whole idea needs the king to take. After 6.Nxf7 nothing defends the knight and the king attacks it. [H] If something defended the knight, Black could not take it, and the fork would win material. The next lesson tests exactly that.

claims.statement: After 6.Nxf7 no white piece defends the knight on f7.
After 6.Nxf7 one black piece (the king) attacks the knight.

steps.chapter: Test yourself and teach it back

steps.prompt: Lichess bands average both players' ratings: White scored 46% where the two averaged 1900 or more, and 57% where they averaged below 1500. What can a result averaged over both players say, and not say, about which player should try this gambit? One sentence.

steps.text: **Say it like this.** [I] 'White's knight on g5 aims at f7. When Black attacks it with a pawn, White can give the knight for a pawn on f7: it forks the queen and a rook, and Black must take it with the king. It is playable only as a trap: the king must take on f7, so White gets the exposed king and the tempi, but the engine still has Black about two pawns ahead.'

steps.prompt: Teach-back: in a few sentences, explain the Alien Gambit to a friend who knows the rules. Say what the knight attacks on f7, why the king must take, why an engine calls it unsound, and one mistake to warn about. Self-check: did you say when it works, when it fails, give an example a beginner could set up, and name a mistake? The app grades nothing; compare with the recap.

fields.label: What it attacks and why Black must take:

steps.text: **Recap.** The knight on g5 aims at f7, defended only by the king. After the pawn attacks it, White can retreat (best) or sacrifice it on f7, forking queen and rook; Black must take with the king. Engine: Black is about two pawns ahead [V, depth 20]. Results follow the rating gap [V, S]. Mistakes: ...Bg4 or ...Ke7 for Black; Qh5+ for White.

steps.prompt: Optional: play a short game from this position as White. Try the retreat once and the sacrifice once, and notice what Black must find.
